title: Audit note on testing Newbold's shorthand proposal
statement: William Romaine Newbold, edited by Roland Grubb Kent, The Cipher of Roger Bacon (1928), open scan at https://oncle-dom.fr/biblio/1928-Newbold-The%20Cipher%20of%20Roger%20Bacon.pdf. Pages 101–103 describe identifying and ordering tiny shorthand marks inside the ink strokes, with Newbold reporting that repeated transcriptions of the same material could differ. Plates XVII–XIX publish his drawings of the marks for three lines of the proposed key. Pages 106–107 give six stages for the shorthand method, with Table IX supplying a shortcut from letter pairs to phonetic values. The first stage requires marks absent from the scorer's EVA and v101 input, and the final stage rearranges the resulting letters into Latin by choosing syntactically and semantically plausible words. The tables specify intermediate conversions. A runnable whole-text claim needs independent mark transcription and a reproducible recomposition rule.
check: Fix plate or canvas coordinates, magnification and a mark inventory before independent annotators transcribe public samples without proposed Latin. Compare agreement on mark identity and order, including repeated annotation of the same crop. If reproducible, freeze the pair conversion and a deterministic recomposition rule and measure the resulting Latin score on independently transcribed text and matched shuffled inputs.
